claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, winter is registered during vernalization through the temperature-dependent repression and epigenetic silencing of floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC).
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, winter is registered during vernalization through the temperature-dependent repression and epigenetic silencing of floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Natural Arabidopsis accessions show considerable variation in vernalization.
source: Natural Arabidopsis accessions show considerable variation in vernalization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous studies.

claim: Variation in autumnal FLC expression influences flowering responses of Arabidopsis accessions resulting in an interplay between promotion and delay of flowering in different climates.
source: This variation influences flowering responses of Arabidopsis accessions resulting in an interplay between promotion and delay of flowering in different climates to balance survival and, through a post-vernalization effect, reproductive output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by field data on flowering time and survival.

claim: Expression variation through non-coding cis variation at FLC has enabled Arabidopsis accessions to adapt to different climatic conditions and year-on-year fluctuations.
source: These data reveal how expression variation through non-coding cis variation at FLC has enabled Arabidopsis accessions to adapt to different climatic conditions and year-on-year fluctuations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the field experiments and genetic analysis.

claim: FLC is a MADS-box transcription factor that delays the transition to flowering in warm temperatures until its expression is downregulated by exposure to cold.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana and its relatives, FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC), a MADS-box transcription factor, delays the transition to flowering in warm temperatures until its expression is downregulated by exposure to cold (Michaels and Amasino, 1999; Sheldon et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: On return to warm, spring-like conditions, FLC remains epigenetically silenced, permitting expression of FT and floral meristem identity genes that trigger the floral transition.
source: On return to warm, spring-like conditions, FLC remains epigenetically silenced, permitting expression of FT and floral meristem identity genes that trigger the floral transition (Helliwell et al., 2006; Searle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: FLC expression is upregulated by the coiled-coil protein FRIGIDA (FRI), which establishes an active transcription state at FLC through interactions with chromatin modifiers including the H3K36 methyltransferase SET DOMAIN GROUP8 (SDG8).
source: FLC expression is upregulated by the coiled-coil protein FRIGIDA (FRI), which establishes an active transcription state at FLC through interactions with chromatin modifiers including the H3K36 methyltransferase SET DOMAIN GROUP8 (SDG8) (Choi et al., 2011; Hyun et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLC upregulation by FRI is antagonised by the autonomous pathway, a group of interacting RNA-processing factors and chromatin modifying factors.
source: This upregulation is antagonised by the autonomous pathway, a group of interacting RNA-processing factors, (eg. FCA and FY) and chromatin modifying factors (eg. FLD and FVE).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The autonomous pathway promotes a low expression state at FLC through interactions with the long non-coding antisense transcript group, COOLAIR.
source: These promote a low expression state at FLC through interactions with the long non-coding antisense transcript group, COOLAIR (Ausín et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cold transcriptionally downregulates FLC, and the locus is maintained in an epigenetically silenced state by a Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) mechanism.
source: Cold transcriptionally downregulates FLC, and the locus is maintained in an epigenetically silenced state by a Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) mechanism (Gendall et al., 2001; Bastow et al., 2004; Sung and Amasino, 2004; Greb et al., 2007; Helliwell et al., 2011; Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PRC2 mechanism requires the temperature-integrating accessory protein, VERNALIZATION INSENSITIVE3 (VIN3).
source: This PRC2 mechanism requires the temperature-integrating accessory protein, VERNALIZATION INSENSITIVE3 (VIN3) (Sung and Amasino, 2004; Bond et al., 2009a; Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cold-induction of VIN3 expression leads to formation of a PHD-PRC2 complex that also contains the PHD protein VERNALIZATION5 (VRN5) and the specific Su(z)12 component VRN2.
source: Cold-induction of VIN3 expression leads to formation of a PHD-PRC2 complex that also contains the PHD protein VERNALIZATION5 (VRN5) and the specific Su(z)12 component VRN2 (Sung et al., 2006a; Greb et al., 2007; De Lucia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PHD-PRC2 complex is nucleated at FLC by the B3-binding protein VP1/ABI3-LIKE 1 (VAL1).
source: This complex is nucleated at FLC by the B3-binding protein VP1/ABI3-LIKE 1 (VAL1) (Qüesta et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The PHD-PRC2 methylates histone H3 lysine 27 residues in a ~ 3 nucleosome domain at FLC to epigenetically 'switch' each allele off in a stochastic manner that over the population of cells produces a quantitative memory of the length of cold.
source: The PHD-PRC2 methylates histone H3 lysine 27 residues in a ~ 3 nucleosome domain at FLC to epigenetically 'switch' each allele off in a stochastic manner that over the population of cells produces a quantitative memory of the length of cold (Angel et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014; Angel et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When plants return to warm conditions, the PHD-PRC2 spreads over the locus to maintain long-term epigenetic memory, and this requires the action of LIKE HETEROCHROMATIN1 (LHP1).
source: When plants return to warm conditions, the PHD-PRC2 spreads over the locus to maintain long-term epigenetic memory, and this requires the action of LIKE HETEROCHROMATIN1 (LHP1) (Mylne et al., 2006; Sung et al., 2006b; Berry et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLC expression and memory is influenced by natural non-coding cis polymorphism at the locus.
source: FLC expression and memory is influenced by natural non-coding cis polymorphism at the locus (Lempe et al., 2005; Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015; Qüesta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different Arabidopsis accessions need different lengths of cold to epigenetically silence FLC, and this requirement is determined by non-coding SNPs at FLC.
source: Different Arabidopsis accessions need different lengths of cold to epigenetically silence FLC, and this requirement is determined by non-coding SNPs at FLC (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within the Arabideae tribe, cis regulation of FLC orthologues contributes to perennial-vs.-annual flowering differences.
source: Indeed, within the Arabideae tribe, cis regulation of FLC orthologues contributes to perennial-vs.-annual flowering differences (Kiefer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Within the worldwide Arabidopsis thaliana population, non-coding variation defines a small number of FLC haplotypes, which confer quantitatively different flowering time responses to different lengths of vernalization in constant cold in the laboratory.
source: Within the worldwide Arabidopsis thaliana population, non-coding variation defines a small number of FLC haplotypes, which confer quantitatively different flowering time responses to different lengths of vernalization in constant cold in the laboratory (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: FLC haplotypes appear to have been maintained in the A. thaliana population due to their contributions to life history diversity.
source: These haplotypes appear to have been maintained in the A. thaliana population due to their contributions to life history diversity (Sánchez-Bermejo et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Méndez-Vigo et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLC haplotypes show different geographic distributions, suggesting that they are adapted to different climates.
source: and they show different geographic distributions, suggesting that they are adapted to different climates (Méndez-Vigo et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The influence of genes of major effect, including FLC, changes depending on the field environment.
source: Such studies have highlighted how the influence of genes of major effect, including FLC, changes depending on the field environment (Wilczek et al., 2009; Fournier-Level et al., 2011; Duncan et al., 2015; Ågren et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous field studies.

claim: Investigation of RNA levels in natura has identified genetic mechanisms in the field that were previously unknown from laboratory observations.
source: In particular, the investigation of RNA levels in natura has identified genetic mechanisms in the field that were previously unknown from laboratory observations (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2018; Song et al., 2018; Nagano et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous field studies.

claim: Field work in Sweden and the UK with the vernalization reference genotype Col FRISF2 and mutants in VIN3 (vin3-4) has shown that initial VIN3-independent FLC downregulation requires cold temperatures, whereas VIN3-mediated epigenetic silencing requires the absence of daily temperatures above 15°C.
source: For example, field work in Sweden and the UK with the vernalization reference genotype Col FRISF2 and mutants in VIN3 (vin3-4) has shown that initial VIN3-independent FLC downregulation requires cold temperatures, whereas VIN3-mediated epigenetic silencing requires the absence of daily temperatures above 15°C (Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous field work.

claim: Autumn conditions greatly influence when epigenetic silencing initiates, sometimes leading to temporal separation of the two phases, which in laboratory constant-condition experiments and some natural environments occur concurrently.
source: Autumn conditions greatly influence when epigenetic silencing initiates, sometimes leading to temporal separation of the two phases, which in laboratory constant-condition experiments and some natural environments occur concurrently (Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous field work.

claim: The three field sites in Norwich, UK, in Ullstorp, Sweden ('South Sweden') and in Ramsta, Sweden ('North Sweden') were chosen to represent climates with different winters.
source: The three field sites in Norwich, UK, in Ullstorp, Sweden ('South Sweden') and in Ramsta, Sweden ('North Sweden') were chosen to represent climates with different winters.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the experimental design.

claim: Norwich has a temperate oceanic climate and a mild winter.
source: Norwich has a temperate oceanic climate and a mild winter
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the field sites.

claim: Ullstorp has a warm-summer continental climate with a winter in which temperatures are often below freezing.
source: Ullstorp has a warm-summer continental climate with a winter in which temperatures are often below freezing
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the field sites.

claim: Ramsta is subarctic, usually with snow cover during winter.
source: and Ramsta is subarctic, usually with snow cover during winter (hence the 0°C flatline in temperatures in Figure 1B; Beck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and supported by temperature data in Figure 1B.

claim: In Norwich 2014–5, substantial VIN3 upregulation did not occur until ~58 days after sowing, although temperature conditions were suitable for VIN3-independent FLC downregulation for most of this time.
source: Previously, we had noted that in 2014–5 in Norwich, substantial VIN3 upregulation did not occur until ~58 days after sowing, although temperature conditions were suitable for VIN3-independent FLC downregulation for most of this time (Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data from the current study.

claim: In the 2016-17 field season in Norwich, VIN3 upregulation was delayed until 48 days after sowing.
source: In the following field season, this pattern occurred again, with VIN3 upregulation delayed until 48 days after sowing (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data from the current study.

claim: For the Col FRI reference, two separate exponential decay curves can be fit to FLC; the first for the initial, slow, VIN3-independent phase and the second for the faster, VIN3-dependent phase of the downregulation.
source: For the Col FRI reference, we had found that we could fit two separate exponential decay curves to FLC; the first for the initial, slow, VIN3-independent phase and the second for the faster, VIN3-dependent phase of the downregulation (Figure 2A; Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Three features of the FLC profile contribute to the level of FLC at any time: the 'Starting level' of FLC before vernalization, the rate of downregulation in the initial VIN3-independent phase, and the rate of VIN3-dependent downregulation.
source: Thus three features of the FLC profile contribute to the level of FLC at any time: firstly the 'Starting level' of FLC before vernalization, secondly the rate of downregulation in the initial VIN3-independent phase, and thirdly the rate of VIN3-dependent downregulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In Norwich 2014–5, the RV FLC accession Edi-0 (haplotype group RV1) behaved very similarly to Col FRI (RV2).
source: In Norwich 2014–5, the RV FLC accession Edi-0 (haplotype group RV1) behaved very similarly to Col FRI (RV2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The SV accessions (Löv-1, Ull2-5, Bro1-6 and Var2-6) show higher levels of FLC throughout the winter compared to Col FRI in Norwich 2014-5.
source: In comparison, the SV accessions (Löv-1, Ull2-5, Bro1-6 and Var2-6) show higher levels of FLC throughout the winter (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ull2-5 started with similar levels of FLC as Col FRI, but slower rates of downregulation in both the VIN3-independent and VIN3-dependent phases generated higher levels of FLC throughout autumn and winter.
source: Ull2-5 started with similar levels of FLC as Col FRI, but slower rates of downregulation in both the VIN3-independent and VIN3-dependent phases generated higher levels of FLC throughout autumn and winter.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: For both Var2-6 and its NIL, an apparently slower VIN3-independent rate of downregulation contributed to a higher FLC level, although the difference in rate is not significant.
source: For both Var2-6 and its NIL, an apparently slower VIN3-independent rate of downregulation contributed to a higher FLC level, although the difference in rate is not significant.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The VIN3-dependent phase was slower in Var2-6 and Löv-1.
source: The VIN3-dependent phase was also slower in Var2-6 and Löv-1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In Sweden 2014–5, at both sites the VIN3-independent and -dependent phases occurred concurrently.
source: In Sweden 2014–5, at both sites the VIN3-independent and -dependent phases occurred concurrently (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and a citation to previous work.

claim: In Sweden 2014-5, there was little variation observed in the overall rate of FLC downregulation between genotypes.
source: There was little variation observed in the overall rate of FLC downregulation between genotypes
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In Sweden 2014-5, most of the natural variation in FLC levels throughout winter was generated by differences in the early expression level.
source: Instead, most of the natural variation in FLC levels throughout winter in Sweden was generated by differences in the early expression level.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In North Sweden 2014-5, both RV accessions had similar Starting levels whereas the SV Swedish accessions were higher to different degrees.
source: In North Sweden again both RV accessions had similar Starting levels whereas the SV Swedish accessions were higher to different degrees.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In South Sweden 2014-5, Löv-1 started with similar levels to Col FRI.
source: However, in South Sweden Löv-1 started with similar levels to Col FRI.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The slower rate of the epigenetic silencing phase in Var2-6 was consistent across years in Norwich.
source: The slower rate of the epigenetic silencing phase in Var2-6 was consistent across years in Norwich (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The change in the VIN3-dependent phase in Var2-6 was consistently mirrored in lower levels of VIN3.
source: Unlike the other accessions, this change in the VIN3-dependent phase in Var2-6 was consistently mirrored in lower levels of VIN3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The circadian clock is an important regulator of VIN3.
source: The circadian clock is an important regulator of VIN3 (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2018; Hepworth et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When sampled over 48 hr in the Norwich field experiment, VIN3 expression in Var2-6 is much lower compared to Col FRI.
source: When sampled over 48 hr in the Norwich field experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), VIN3 expression in Var2-6 is much lower compared to our previous results from Col FRI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,D; Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The expression of circadian clock component CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED1 (CCA1) is lower in Var2-6 compared to Col FRI.
source: as is the expression of circadian clock component CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED1, the protein of which binds to the VIN3 promoter (CCA1; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and a citation.

claim: Variation in the circadian clock may underlie some of the difference in FLC regulation in Var2-6.
source: Therefore, variation in the circadian clock may underlie some of the difference in FLC regulation in Var2-6.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on VIN3 and CCA1 expression.

claim: vin3 mutants (vin3-4, vin3-1) did not show the increase in downregulation rate that marks the later epigenetic phase of silencing.
source: As previously reported (Hepworth et al., 2018), vin3 mutants (vin3-4, vin3-1) did not show the increase in downregulation rate that marks the later epigenetic phase of silencing (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutants defective in epigenetic memory (vrn1-4, vrn2-1, vrn5-8, lhp1-3) did not show the increase in downregulation rate that marks the later epigenetic phase of silencing.
source: This effect was also seen for other mutants defective in epigenetic memory; vrn1-4; vrn2-1 (defective in the Su(z)12 homologue component of PRC2); vrn5-8 (defective in the VIN3-related protein VRN5); and lhp1-3, in accordance with this phase being required for epigenetic silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of the H3K36 methyltransferase sdg8 generated the same effect as vin3 mutants, correlated with its delayed upregulation of VIN3.
source: Loss of the H3K36 methyltransferase sdg8 generated the same effect, correlated with its delayed upregulation of VIN3 (Kim et al., 2010; Jean Finnegan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the initial, VIN3-independent silencing phase, both Col fri (Col-0) and sdg8 FRI were hyper-responsive, consistent with a role for SDG8 with FRI in the establishment of the high FLC expression state.
source: In the initial, VIN3-independent silencing phase, both Col fri (Col-0) and sdg8 FRI were hyper-responsive, consistent with a role for SDG8 with FRI in the establishment of the high FLC expression state (Hyun et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutants in the autonomous pathway (fca-9, fld-4 and fve-3) had no significant effect on VIN3-independent silencing, but behaved mostly like Col FRI.
source: Mutants in the autonomous pathway, fca-9, fld-4 and fve-3, which upregulate FLC expression in the absence of FRI, had no significant effect on VIN3-independent silencing, but behaved mostly like Col FRI
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The mutant with the most reduced VIN3-independent response was the B3-binding transcription factor VAL1, required for PRC2 action at FLC.
source: The mutant with the most reduced VIN3-independent response was the B3-binding transcription factor VAL1, required for PRC2 action at FLC (Figure 4E; Qüesta et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to previous studies.

claim: The vrn mutants, vrn1-4 and vrn5-8, showed reduced VIN3-independent response, followed closely by a non-significant but consistent trend for vrn2-1.
source: followed closely by the vrn mutants, vrn1-4 and vrn5-8, and a non-significant but consistent trend for vrn2-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The lhp1-3 and vin3 mutants do not show clear impairment in the early phase of downregulation.
source: Conversely, the lhp1-3 and vin3 mutants do not show clear impairment in the early phase of downregulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Chromatin modifiers are required for both phases of downregulation in the field.
source: Overall, it seems that chromatin modifiers are required for both phases of downregulation in the field.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant analysis data in Figure 4.

claim: In Sweden, the starting levels are significantly more variable than the shutdown rates.
source: In Sweden, the starting levels are significantly more variable than the shutdown rates (p-value=2.8⋅10-8 for the first year, Figure 5A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In Norwich, the VIN3-independent shutdown rate is more variable than the starting levels and VIN3-dependent rate.
source: but in Norwich, the VIN3-independent shutdown rate is more variable than the starting levels and VIN3-dependent rate (p-value=2.1⋅10-5 for 2014, p-value=5.0⋅10-4 for 2016, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Combining Norwich and Sweden data, the early shutdown rate is most variable.
source: Combining Norwich and Sweden data, the early shutdown rate is again most variable (p-value=1.9⋅10-10 for 2014, p-value=2.0⋅10-5 for 2016, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the variability of the starting levels between the different field sites and years.
source: On the other hand, there was no significant difference in the variability of the starting levels (Figure 5D) between the different field sites and years
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The combination of starting levels and rate of VIN3-independent shutdown, called 'autumnal expression', provides most of the variation in FLC levels between accessions and NILs.
source: Therefore, it seems that the combination of these two determinants (starting levels and rate of VIN3-independent shutdown), which together we call 'autumnal expression', provides most of the variation in FLC levels between these accessions and NILs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of variation in FLC regulation.

claim: In the 2014–5 season, all accessions and NILs bolted relatively synchronously in spring in Norwich and Sweden.
source: In the 2014–5 season, all accessions and NILs bolted relatively synchronously in spring in Norwich and Sweden, although there were small but significant differences in both cases.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: In Norwich 2014-5, the flowering time difference between the NILs and Col FRI was small.
source: In Norwich, the flowering time difference between the NILs and Col FRI was small
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Sweden 2014-5, the flowering time difference between the NILs and Col FRI was not significant.
source: and in Sweden not significant, suggesting that most of the variation seen between the accessions did not derive from the FLC haplotype (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).

claim: There was very little difference in branch production in the NILs and accessions in Norwich 2014-5.
source: There was also very little difference in branch production in the NILs and accessions in Norwich (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Branch production in Norwich 2014-5 was surprisingly low, despite the known role of FLC in suppressing branching.
source: which was surprisingly low, despite the known role of FLC in suppressing branching (Huang et al., 2013; Lazaro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Longer vernalization times resulted in increased numbers of branches in controlled condition experiments.
source: Nevertheless, we confirmed that this effect does occur in the accessions and NILs in controlled condition experiments, in which longer vernalization times resulted in increased numbers of branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was wide variation and substantial delay to bolting within the genotypes for plants transferred to the warm greenhouses early in autumn, at all sites, indicating that vernalization requirement had not been saturated at this point.
source: There was wide variation and substantial delay to bolting within the genotypes for plants transferred to the warm greenhouses early in autumn, at all sites, indicating that vernalization requirement had not been saturated at this point (Figure 6A,C,E).

claim: Some genotypes (particularly Löv-1) required more than 46 days in the field before most individuals were competent to flower in warm, long-day conditions.
source: Some genotypes (particularly Löv-1) required more than 46 days in the field before most individuals were competent to flower in warm, long-day conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: As winter progressed, time to bolt after transfer reduced quantitatively and became more uniform for plants within and between each genotype.
source: However, as winter progressed, time to bolt after transfer reduced quantitatively and became more uniform for plants within and between each genotype (Figure 6B,D,F)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6B, D, F.

claim: All accessions and NILs bolted broadly synchronously and rapidly after removal on 21st December in Norwich.
source: All accessions and NILs bolted broadly synchronously and rapidly after removal on 21st December in Norwich

claim: In North Sweden NILs and accessions were almost synchronous by 24th November.
source: in North Sweden NILs and accessions were almost synchronous by 24th November, in line with previous findings (Duncan et al., 2015)

claim: In South Sweden FRI-containing lines were broadly synchronous by the last transfer on 17th December.
source: and in South Sweden FRI-containing lines were broadly synchronous by the last transfer on 17th December (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 3–4).

claim: In current climates almost all Arabidopsis plants have probably saturated their requirement for vernalization before midwinter, ensuring that flowering time is not delayed the following spring.
source: Therefore, in current climates almost all Arabidopsis plants have probably saturated their requirement for vernalization before midwinter, ensuring that flowering time is not delayed the following spring.

claim: Across genotypes, in Norwich and North Sweden 2016–7, the time to the floral transition after transfer from the field correlated closely with FLC expression at the time of transfer.
source: Across genotypes, in Norwich and North Sweden 2016–7, the time to the floral transition after transfer from the field correlated closely with FLC expression at the time of transfer, as expected (Norwich, R2 = 0.68, p<0.001, North Sweden, R2 = 0.85, p<0.001, linear regression Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6G, H.

claim: Accessions, NILs and mutants with high starting levels and slower downregulation rates generally bolted later and took longer to saturate their vernalization requirement.
source: Accessions, NILs and mutants with high starting levels and slower downregulation rates generally bolted later and took longer to saturate their vernalization requirement, indicating that the variation in FLC dynamics in autumn has a phenotypic effect.

claim: Each accession differed in the relationship between FLC levels at transfer and subsequent bolting time.
source: However, each accession differed in the relationship between FLC levels at transfer and subsequent bolting time (Figure 6—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 5–6.

claim: For Löv-1 and the Löv NIL1, the time to bolt for a given level of FLC at transfer is longer than for Col FRI.
source: For example, for Löv-1 and the Löv NIL1, the time to bolt for a given level of FLC at transfer is longer than for Col FRI
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 5–6.

claim: For Edi-0, the time to bolt for a given level of FLC at transfer is shorter than for Col FRI.
source: but for Edi-0, it is shorter (Figure 6—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 5–6.

claim: The FLC-post-vern value (m) represents the slope of the regression between FLC spliced RNA levels at the time of transfer to the subsequent floral transition time for these transferred plants.
source: We named this feature the FLC-post-vern value (m in Table 1, days-to-bolting-per-FLC-unit), representing the slope of the regression between FLC spliced RNA levels at the time of transfer (x-axis) to the subsequent floral transition time for these transferred plants (y-axis, as for Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 6G, H.

claim: For a given level of FLC at the time of transfer, a genotype with a higher m 'post-vern' value flowers later than one with a lower m value.
source: This means that, for a given level of FLC at the time of transfer, a genotype with a higher m 'post-vern' value flowers later than one with a lower m value.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an explanation of the FLC-post-vern value.

claim: There was substantial variation between the different glasshouses in the estimates for the accessions of the FLC-post-vern value, suggesting that there is a large genotype-by-environment effect on this parameter due to non-FLC effects.
source: There was substantial variation between the different glasshouses in the estimates for the accessions (Table 1), suggesting that there is a large genotype-by-environment effect on this parameter due to non-FLC effects.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Within the lines in the common Col FRI background, the estimates of FLC-post-vern value correlated more closely across the two glasshouse environments, with the exception of the Ull NIL.
source: Within the lines in the common Col FRI background, the estimates correlated more closely across the two glasshouse environments, with the exception of the Ull NIL.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Within the Col FRI background, the FLC haplotypes have different effects after vernalization, as well as different responses to vernalization.
source: Therefore, within the Col FRI background, we can quantify the effect of FLC levels on bolting time in warm, long-photoperiod environments, and find that the FLC haplotypes have different effects after vernalization, as well as different responses to vernalization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The FLC-post-vern effect may be linked to reactivation of FLC expression in the warm, as the vin3-1 and Löv-1 NIL1, both of which have reactivation phenotypes, have high 'post-vern' values.
source: This effect may be linked to reactivation of FLC expression in the warm, as the vin3-1 and Löv-1 NIL1, both of which have reactivation phenotypes (Sung and Amasino, 2004; Duncan et al., 2015; Qüesta et al., 2020), have high 'post-vern' values.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Table 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: At all sites in the 2014–5 season, and in South Sweden in 2016–7, across all accessions and NILs, flowering in the field occurred after midwinter.
source: At all sites in the 2014–5 season, and in South Sweden in 2016–7, across all accessions and NILs, flowering in the field occurred after midwinter (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: By midwinter, FLC levels were below the level at which they influenced flowering time in the transfers.
source: by which time FLC levels were below the level at which they influenced flowering time in the transfers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6.

claim: In the warm North Sweden autumn 2016–7 many of the plants with the Col background (NILs, Col FRI, and vin3-1 FRI) transitioned to flowering early, by the 18th November, before winter and snowfall.
source: However, in the warm North Sweden autumn 2016–7 many of the plants with the Col background (NILs, Col FRI, and vin3-1 FRI) transitioned to flowering early, by the 18th November, before winter and snowfall (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: Precocious bolting before winter was rare in the SV accessions and was much reduced even in the RV accession Edi-0.
source: This precocious bolting was rare in the SV accessions and was much reduced even in the RV accession Edi-0.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: Over all the genotypes, the percentage of plants transitioning to flowering before winter negatively correlated with genotype FLC expression on 5th October.
source: Over all the genotypes, the percentage of plants transitioning to flowering before winter negatively correlated with genotype FLC expression on 5th October, one day after the first recorded bolting for plants in the field (p<0.001, Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) for binomial data, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7B.

claim: The negative correlation between precocious flowering and FLC expression occurred before substantial upregulation of VIN3, indicating that this variation in FLC must derive from the combination of the starting levels and VIN3-independent shutdown.
source: This was before substantial upregulation of VIN3, indicating that this variation in FLC must derive from the combination of the starting levels and VIN3-independent shutdown.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the Col FRISF2 background the Var and Löv FLC haplotypes, the NILs with the highest FLC levels during autumn, substantially reduced precocious bolting.
source: Within the Col FRISF2 background the Var and Löv FLC haplotypes, the NILs with the highest FLC levels during autumn (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), substantially reduced precocious bolting (p=0.005, binomial proportions test, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variation in FLC starting expression and shutdown (collectively called autumnal expression) results in variation in the alignment of flowering with the seasons.
source: Thus, variation in FLC starting expression and shutdown (collectively called autumnal expression) results in variation in the alignment of flowering with the seasons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on precocious flowering in North Sweden 2016-7.

claim: Across all genotypes, plants that bolted precociously were not observed to set seed before winter.
source: Across all genotypes, plants that bolted precociously were not observed to set seed before winter.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by field observations.

claim: In North Sweden 2016, mortality was high, compared to other years and sites.
source: In this year (2016) and at this site (N.Sweden), mortality was high, compared to other years and sites
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Plants that bolted precociously were less likely to survive the winter (42% of bolting plants survived, whereas 67% of non-bolting plants survived to spring).
source: and plants that bolted precociously were less likely to survive the winter (42% of bolting plants survived, whereas 67% of non-bolting plants survived to spring, p<0.001, binomial proportions test, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: High FLC levels in October correlated with higher survival to seed set in the field.
source: Therefore, high FLC levels in October correlated with higher survival to seed set in the field (p<0.003, GLM for binomial data, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Despite many of the NILs having a high level of precocious flowering, several NILs produced more seed than the locally-adapted accessions.
source: Despite many of the NILs having a high level of precocious flowering, several NILs produced more seed than the locally-adapted accessions (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the Col FRI background plants, there was no overall penalty in average silique number for individual surviving plants that bolted before winter compared to those that transitioned afterwards.
source: In the Col FRI background plants, there was no overall penalty in average silique number for individual surviving plants that bolted before winter compared to those that transitioned afterwards (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Saturating vernalization increased seed set in the 2016 Norwich transfer experiments, as plants that were transferred before saturation of vernalization requirement produced lower and more variable amounts of seed.
source: Saturating vernalization increased seed set in the 2016 Norwich transfer experiments, as plants that were transferred before saturation of vernalization requirement produced lower and more variable amounts of seed (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: In the field in North Sweden 2017 silique production occurred only after winter, after saturation of vernalization requirement.
source: However, in the field in North Sweden 2017 silique production occurred only after winter, after saturation of vernalization requirement (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: Within the Col FRI background, the average silique set among survivors correlated with rosette branching.
source: Within the Col FRI background, the average silique set among survivors correlated with rosette branching (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2G)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Branch number was strongly negatively correlated with FLC-post-vern, though not FLC expression.
source: and branch number was strongly negatively correlated with FLC-post-vern, though not FLC expression (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Survival was the principle factor explaining total silique production.
source: As expected, survival was the principle factor explaining total silique production (Figure 7—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2I.

claim: When combined with survival to seed set, the post-vern value of FLC explained a large part of the variation in genotype fitness in Col FRI background.
source: However, we found that although the post-vern value of FLC did not well explain total genotype fitness on its own (Figure 7F), when combined with survival to seed set both factors explained a large part of the variation in genotype fitness in Col FRI background (linear model adjusted R2 = 0.94, p-value=0.001 for model, post-vern p-value=0.006, percentage survival to silique set p-value=0.002, Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2I.

claim: In 2014–5, winter conditions in Norwich generated a subtly different response to those in Sweden, activating the VIN3-independent transcriptional shutdown before the VIN3-dependent epigenetic pathway.
source: However, in 2014–5, winter conditions in Norwich generated a subtly different response to those in Sweden, activating the VIN3-independent transcriptional shutdown before the VIN3-dependent epigenetic pathway (delay in VIN3 onset and slow then fast shutdown of FLC in Norwich, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the 2016-17 season, the pattern of delayed VIN3 upregulation was triggered again, not only in Norwich, but also in North Sweden.
source: In the following season, this pattern was triggered again, not only in Norwich, but also in North Sweden, implying that this is a common occurrence that plants must adjust to across climates, although with different frequencies at different locations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variation in FLC mRNA levels in both accessions and NILs is largely due to differences in both the starting FLC level and the VIN3-independent rate of shutdown (collectively called autumnal expression), which vary widely between accessions but not between field sites or years.
source: We find that variation in FLC mRNA levels in both accessions and NILs is largely due to differences in both the starting FLC level and the VIN3-independent rate of shutdown (collectively called autumnal expression), which vary widely between accessions but not between field sites or years (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Variation in rate of response, as well as absolute levels of FLC, partly explains why FLC levels measured at any one time may not correlate with the final flowering time phenotype in different accessions.
source: This variation in rate of response, as well as absolute levels of FLC, partly explains why FLC levels measured at any one time may not correlate with the final flowering time phenotype in different accessions (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutants of the autonomous pathway generally behaved in a similar manner to Col FRI in terms of vernalization response.
source: Mutants of the autonomous pathway, which increase FLC expression in fri plants in laboratory conditions (Ausín et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2016), generally behaved in a similar manner to Col FRI in terms of vernalization response (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to previous studies.

claim: All three factors that set FLC levels in the field (starting levels, VIN3-independent and VIN3-dependent phases) require chromatin modifiers for their correct function.
source: All three factors that set FLC levels in the field (starting levels, VIN3-independent and VIN3-dependent phases) require chromatin modifiers for their correct function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The VIN3-dependent (epigenetic) phase is the least variable among natural accessions.
source: In the natural accessions we find that the VIN3-dependent (epigenetic) phase is indeed the least variable (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The low variability of the VIN3-dependent phase may explain why so much variation in vernalization maps to FLC itself.
source: This may explain why so much variation in vernalization maps to FLC itself (Lempe et al., 2005; Sánchez-Bermejo et al., 2012; Dittmar et al., 2014; Sasaki et al., 2015; Bloomer and Dean, 2017; Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: QTLs over the VIN3 region have previously been found to affect flowering.
source: Nevertheless, we did observe variation in VIN3 expression in Var2-6, which seems to derive from differences in circadian regulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and QTLs over the VIN3 region have previously been found to affect flowering (Dittmar et al., 2014; Méndez-Vigo et al., 2016; Ågren et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The importance of FLC variation in adaptation for natural populations is well established.
source: The importance of FLC variation in adaptation for natural populations is well established (Méndez-Vigo et al., 2011; Sánchez-Bermejo et al., 2012; Dittmar et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Duncan et al., 2015; Ågren et al., 2017; Bloomer and Dean, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Even in a challengingly warm year, vernalization requirement saturated before midwinter across three climates.
source: However, we found that even in a challengingly warm year, vernalization requirement saturated before midwinter across three climates (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The saturation of vernalization requirement before midwinter is a general response in all tested accessions.
source: However, we find that this is a general response in all our tested accessions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The vin3 and vrn mutants had notably delayed flowering in both years at the Norwich site.
source: The principle exceptions were the vin3 and vrn mutants, which had notably delayed flowering in both years at the Norwich site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Incomplete vernalization leads to delayed flowering and reduced fecundity.
source: The consequences of incomplete vernalization are severe – in our 2016–7 transfer experiments this led to delayed flowering and reduced fecundity (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: Several field experiments have found a general trend towards earlier flowering promoting fitness in environments with warmer winters.
source: and several field experiments have found a general trend towards earlier flowering promoting fitness in environments with warmer winters (Ågrena et al., 2013; Fournier-Level et al., 2013; Grillo et al., 2013; Dittmar et al., 2014; Ågren et al., 2017; Exposito-Alonso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous field studies.

claim: In 2014–5, the high synchronicity of flowering in all the accessions and NILs after winter and the fact that flowering aligned with spring across field sites suggests that in most plants vernalization has adapted to reduce the delaying effect of FLC on flowering as early as possible.
source: In 2014–5, the high synchronicity of flowering in all the accessions and NILs after winter and the fact that flowering aligned with spring across our field sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggests that in most plants vernalization has adapted to reduce the delaying effect of FLC on flowering as early as possible.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Swedish, cold-winter-adapted accessions and FLC haplotypes associated with slow vernalization expressed the highest FLC levels throughout autumn and early winter.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that the Swedish, cold-winter-adapted accessions and FLC haplotypes associated with slow vernalization expressed the highest FLC levels throughout autumn and early winter (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In North Sweden in 2016–7, a relatively warm September with a long period with less precipitation required watering of the plants to avoid drought stress.
source: There was a relatively warm September that year with a long period with less precipitation (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute, 2020, www.smhi.se/data/meteorologi/ladda-ner-meteorologiska-observationer), which required us to water the plants to avoid drought stress.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to meteorological data.

claim: In plants with a haplotype characteristic of a slow-vernalizing accession, including the locally-adapted Swedish accessions, the higher level of FLC expression protected against precocious flowering and its consequent reduced survival.
source: In our experiments, in plants with a haplotype characteristic of a slow-vernalizing accession, including the locally-adapted Swedish accessions, the higher level of FLC expression protected against precocious flowering and its consequent reduced survival (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effects of FLC haplotypes are only revealed occasionally, which is a logical consequence of the fact that the flowering time genes can have strong or weak effects depending on the environment.
source: However, that the effects of these haplotypes are only revealed occasionally is a logical consequence of the fact that the flowering time genes can have strong or weak effects depending on the environment (Wilczek et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2015; Burghardt et al., 2016; Fournier-Level et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2018; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLC also controls fecundity as well as survival.
source: FLC also controls fecundity as well as survival (Ågrena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Li et al., 2014 found that FLC haplotypes from SV accessions produced lower seed weight compared to those from RV accessions in non-saturating vernalization conditions.
source: Li et al., 2014 found that FLC haplotypes from SV accessions produced lower seed weight compared to those from RV accessions in non-saturating vernalization conditions, though the mechanism for this effect is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the field, silique production is closely linked to branch production.
source: In the field, silique production is closely linked to branch production (Figure 7; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 7 and a citation to a previous study.

claim: In Arabidopsis, saturation of vernalization requirement is known to increase flowering branch production, particularly rosette branch production, and this effect is linked to FLC.
source: In Arabidopsis, saturation of vernalization requirement is known to increase flowering branch production, particularly rosette branch production, and this effect is linked to FLC (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2; Huang et al., 2013; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Under the conditions in the field in North Sweden, branch production was negatively related to the FLC post-vern factor.
source: However, we found that under the conditions in the field in North Sweden, branch production was negatively related to a factor we named 'FLC post-vern', which encoded the relationship between FLC levels and subsequent flowering in warm controlled conditions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Variation in the FLC post-vern factor probably derives from regulatory differences at FLC post-cold, such as the reactivation phenotype of the Löv-1 FLC allele.
source: Variation in this factor probably derives from regulatory differences at FLC post-cold, such as the reactivation phenotype of the Löv-1 FLC allele (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012; Duncan et al., 2015; Qüesta et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLC repression of flowering can saturate at the shoot apical and axillary meristems at different rates, a phenomenon that occurs in the perennial relative Arabis alpina.
source: allowing FLC repression of flowering to saturate at the shoot apical and axillary meristems at different rates, a phenomenon that occurs in the perennial relative Arabis alpina (Wang et al., 2009; Lazaro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Autumnal FLC expression, made up from FLC starting levels and early phases of FLC silencing, is the major determinant for variation in FLC levels during vernalization.
source: Autumnal FLC expression, made up from FLC starting levels and early phases of FLC silencing, is the major determinant for variation in FLC levels during vernalization (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: FLC downregulation aligns flowering response to spring and non-coding variation affects this alignment in different climatic conditions and year-on-year fluctuations in natural temperature profiles.
source: FLC downregulation aligns flowering response to spring and non-coding variation affects this alignment in different climatic conditions and year-on-year fluctuations in natural temperature profiles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data from the field experiments.
